about: The stops and attractions framing the 1925 streetcar map: one box each, numbered clockwise from the top left. Each note is written from the sources listed with it; `at` is the point the box is centered on, `line` the car line that served it in 1925. Voice: an invitation to ride as of 1925 (where to board, what you would find), then what became of the place, in the past tense; every fact is from the sources listed.

stops.title: Westhampton Park
stops.note: Ride the Westhampton car out Grove Avenue to the end of the line. The streetcar company opened an amusement park by the lake in May 1902, a little Eiffel Tower and all, but it never paid. Richmond College bought the grounds in 1910 and moved here by 1914.

stops.title: State Fair Grounds
stops.note: Take the State Fair Grounds spur up the Boulevard to the fair. The State Fair came back here in 1906, opening with an airshow, and built its exhibition hall in 1908; races run on the fair's own track. The fair moved out in 1941, and The Diamond stands on the ground today.

stops.title: Ginter Park
stops.line: Lakeside line and the Ashland interurban
stops.note: Lewis Ginter, who made his fortune in cigarettes, began buying Northside land in the late 1880s, and Ginter Park became one of Richmond's first streetcar suburbs. Stay aboard the Chamberlayne cars for his Lakeside Park, just north of this view: a lake, a small zoo and a nine-hole golf course.

stops.title: Barton Heights
stops.line: Lakeside line, over the First Street viaduct
stops.note: Cross the valley of Bacon's Quarter Branch on the First Street viaduct. James Barton had it built so a car could leave for Broad Street every 20 minutes. Begun in 1894, it was one of the first trolley suburbs in the country: a Henrico town from 1896, and part of Richmond since 1914.

stops.title: Highland Park
stops.line: Highland Park line, over the Fifth Street viaduct
stops.note: Over the Fifth Street viaduct and round the loop at the top of the hill. The advertisements promise fresh air and under 15 minutes by trolley to Seventh and Broad. Run through to Hull Street, the Highland Park cars would outlast every other line in town: the last one ran on 25 November 1949.

stops.title: Nine Mile Road
stops.line: Venable Street line, toward Seven Pines
stops.note: Out the old New Bridge Road toward Seven Pines. The Richmond City and Seven Pines Railway laid its track here in 1888 and electrified it in 1892, two years after Highland Springs was founded along the way. In 1918 the government bought the line to carry workers to a wartime powder-bagging plant.

stops.title: Church Hill and Jefferson Park
stops.line: Marshall Street and Jefferson Avenue lines
stops.note: Since 1911 the Marshall Street Viaduct has carried the cars across Shockoe Valley to the hill where Richmond was first laid out. In October 1925 the railroad tunnel under Jefferson Park caved in during repairs, killing at least three men. They lie inside it still.

stops.title: Seventh and Broad
stops.note: Every line comes downtown. In May 1888 Frank Sprague, $75,000 of his own money spent, finished the Clay Street line: the first electric street railway in the world that truly worked. By 1925, Seventh and Broad is the corner every suburb measures its ride against.

stops.title: Manchester
stops.line: Hull Street line, over the Mayo Bridge
stops.note: Across the river on the Mayo Bridge. Manchester was a city of its own until it joined Richmond in 1910, on the promise of a better bridge. The arched concrete span of 1913, drawn here as a plain deck, brings the cars from 14th Street straight onto Hull Street, Manchester's main street.

stops.title: Woodland Heights
stops.line: Forest Hill line, down Semmes Avenue
stops.note: Down the middle of Semmes Avenue. The Southside Land and Improvement Company bought the old Rhodes place in 1889, sold lots to the east and north, and opened a car line in 1890 to fill them. The trolley, and the park at the end of it, were the suburb's best selling points.

stops.title: Forest Hill Park
stops.line: Forest Hill line, end of the line
stops.note: The end of the line, and Richmond's favorite trolley park since 1890, with a boat lake, a bath house and the Dip-the-Dips roller coaster; only the lake is drawn. Its days are numbered: the coaster was condemned in 1931, the rides came down in 1932, and in 1934 the city bought the 105 acres for a park.

stops.title: Byrd Park
stops.note: Down Robinson Street and out Lakeview Avenue. The city laid out the park around its new reservoir from 1874 and named it for William Byrd by 1907. Next door, the Idlewood amusement park opened at the end of the line in 1906, with a horse-show pavilion and lit lagoons. It was gone by 1914.

stops.title: The Fan
stops.line: Main Street, Floyd Avenue and Broad Street lines
stops.note: Cars run west through the Fan on Main Street, Floyd Avenue and Broad Street, and houses have filled the blocks between them: one of Richmond's first streetcar suburbs. The city's 1906 annexation came, as one historian puts it, "in direct response to the trolley." The Floyd Avenue cars run on to Westhampton.

stops.title: Broad and Laurel
stops.note: Board the interurban here for Lakeside and Ashland. Opened in July 1907 for big, fast electric cars, the line leaves its terminal from the second floor, on a half-mile concrete viaduct over the Seaboard's tracks. Reorganized as the Richmond–Ashland Railway, it ran until 1938. The terminal building still stands.
